method: one Metal kernel, one dispatch, for rows up to 256 elements: a register-resident thread per row for rows up to 64 (and for every tall block, which needs the thread count), a 64-lane threadgroup per row above that (and for short blocks of 17-64 elements, which need the parallelism); otherwise stable sort + run length in MPS aten ops. No CPU fallback, no per-element Python and no data-dependent host read: float rows always run the NaN-segment double argsort, integer rows a single stable sort

contract.convention: most frequent value, ties to the smallest value, reported at the last occurrence of that value in the row; NaN-free rows only for the last-occurrence clause

cpu_parity.note: the CPU kernel reproduces its own output only up to this row length on this machine; above it its std::sort reorders equal keys and its NaN placement depends on an introsort partition that compares values only, so both the reported index and, on NaN rows, the reported value are unspecified.  The overlay's defined result is the one in ``contract``; every place it departs from what CPU happened to print is listed under ``cpu_parity`` and none of them is folded into a pass flag.

gradient.method: torch.mode(values).backward(random grad) on a leaf, compared with the CPU leaf

timings.method: median and min of 25 reps after 5 warmups, torch.mps.synchronize() around each MPS rep, best of three passes, speedups from min; the machine was shared with other agents, so trust the relative order more than the absolute numbers
timings.burst_method: min of 15 rounds of 10 calls between two torch.mps.synchronize() calls, after 3 warmup rounds; this is the per-call dispatch and GPU cost, with the ~60 us submit-and-wait round trip that dominates a single short call divided out

dispatch_floor.what: tiny.add(1) on 8 elements: one dispatch plus one synchronize, no work worth measuring
